blocks.text: It is demonstrated that שפן saphan is not the rabbit, as they maintain, but a kind of larger mouse found in Eretz Yisrael, Egypt, and Libya, which Herodotus and others call Δίπους [Dipous], the Elders Χοιρογρύλλιος [Choirogryllios], Jerome Ἀρκτομῦς [Arktomys], and the Arabs اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, concerning which much previously unpublished information is presented from the writings of the Arabs.

In Levit, XI, 5. and Deut. XIV, 7., השפן, ὁ σαφάν [ho saphan], is listed with the camel and the hare among those animals which do indeed chew the cud, but [col. 1002] do not have a cloven hoof, and are therefore unclean. The plural שפנים sephanim occurs in Psal. CIV. 18. The rock is a refuge לשפנים, τοῖς σεφανίμ [tois sephanim]. And in Prov. XXX, 26., שפנים sephanim are a feeble people; they make their home in the rock. Most more recent writers interpret this as rabbits. Many things appear to support this interpretation. 1. In the Law השפן is twice joined with הארנבת, that is, with the hare, as an animal of the same kind. 2. The passage of the Psalm which we have just cited is rendered thus in the Greek edition: Πέτρα καταφυγὴ τοῖς λαγωοῖς [Petra kataphygē tois lagōois], The rock is a refuge for hares. Some copies have τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις [tois choirogrylliois], that is, as they maintain, for hedgehogs. But the most ancient writers follow the former reading. Jerome, in Letter 135 to Sunnia and Fretela: All translated χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious] with a similar word; the LXX alone interpreted it as hares. Theodoret also read it thus in his Commentary on this Psalm, as did Basil in chapter 2 of his work on Isaiah, and Apollinaris in his Paraphrase,
Πέτροις ἠλιβάτοις περιθάρσεες εἰσὶ λαγωοὶ [Petrois ēlibatois peritharsees eisi lagōoi],

Hares put their trust in steep rocks. So too the Arabic version, which was translated from the Greek: The rocks are a refuge الارانب [al-arānib] for hares. Others combine both, as Augustine does on this passage: The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares. Arnobius: There is the rock, providing a refuge either for the young of hedgehogs, etc., or for hares. Bede, on Proverbs, chapter 30: And it should be noted that in the Psalm, where we sing: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs,” some manuscripts have for hares, and some have for choerogryllii. 3. The Hebrew of Prov. XXX, 26., שפנים עם לא עצום, was translated thus by the Vulgate translator: The little hare is a feeble people. He was following, if I am not mistaken, [II, 410] some Greek translator who had interpreted שפנים as λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, that is, rabbits. For in Strabo, book 3, λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, is used for rabbits. The Greeks have no other name for the rabbit. For κόνιλος [konilos] in Aelian and κούνικλος [kouniklos] in Polybius and Galen were words peculiar to the Spaniards, while λεβηρὶς [lebēris] in Strabo and Erotian was peculiar to the Massiliots; they were not used in Greece. 4. The ancient Nominum liber, which they attribute to Philo, has the following under Jeremiah: SAPHAN, choerogryllius, hare, or hedgehog. And under Ezekiel: SAPHAN, hedgehog, or hare. 5. In the Arabic Lexicon of Giggeius, p. 854, vol. 2, سفن [sfn] saphan is rendered rabbit. But I have no idea where he obtained this, for I have found it nowhere else. 6. The Hebrew name שפן saphan seems to allude to the Hebrew verbs ספן and צפן, the former of which means to cover, the latter to hide. And it seems to suit the rabbit, which seeks hiding places in holes, so that it may hide in them and be, as it were, covered. Martial:
The rabbit delights in dwelling in excavated caves.
